An imprecise scalar permits verifier state pruning to skip a nonzero store path. mark_chain_precision repairs kernel validation of submitted programs; no exported-header or user compiler change is described.
The kernel verifier predicts the wrong branch because it ignores comparison width; the example BPF program supplies input to verification rather than userspace implementation.
The unbounded scan runs in the kernel NVMe workqueue against device-reported namespace IDs. A storage target supplies data, while the CPU-consuming loop is the host driver implementation.

The description explains a kernel verifier checkpoint that loses outer-frame precision and can accept unsafe programs. The callback program is input; precision backtracking is the vulnerable kernel implementation.
The omitted edge mixes caller precision marks with callee instructions in kernel verifier state; the description locates failure during verification.
The corruption concerns live kernel classifier nodes, hash tables and IDR reservations. Administrative filter requests trigger it but do not make the allocator part of userspace headers.

Incorrect counting allows the kernel request builder to overrun its SCID array. Concurrent socket connections are inputs to kernel channel management; the fix does not redefine the on-wire request layout.
Shared kernel session objects are freed while other channels still use them; internal session/cache headers support coordinated teardown.
The error is in kernel verifier reasoning about branch register states before executing a BPF program. Pointer-type flags are internal verification metadata, not an exported userspace implementation.

Shared shadow pages can be incorrectly marked unsynchronized when only one address space is checked. The affected operation is hypervisor MMU bookkeeping; no exported guest-memory layout or userspace header behavior is described.
The kernel SMB receive path validates against an entire decrypted frame instead of the current submessage; wire data is input to this parser.

The stale node spans kernel task/PID reassignment and timer teardown during exec failure. execve and timer calls are entry points; the queue and task ownership are kernel runtime state.

A nested-guest object loses its final reference while another vCPU uses it outside the lock. Pinning that kernel object around per-guest work fixes the hypervisor lifetime race; guest actions are triggers only.
The kernel wireless operation can confuse an AP station with a TDLS peer and corrupt station lifecycle assumptions; no exported-code effect is described.
A failed interface startup leaves a kernel timer active until its storage is freed. The affected implementation is the wireless driver lifecycle, not a userspace LED control header.

Completion toward userspace is reported before asynchronous driver completion releases ownership. The kernel must delay freeing the request; userspace notification does not imply a userspace implementation.
A reference keeps the kernel object allocated but not operational; the fix synchronizes registration-state checks with the callback.
Concurrent link deletion frees a net_device used by kernel route construction. Netlink deletion or packet sending are external triggers, not a userspace implementation of that reference acquisition.

records.unchanged_applicability_basis: Overflow lets a remote range pass the kernel region check and produce an invalid page-array index. The repair changes runtime address validation in RXE, not exported RDMA declarations.

The primary fix concerns kernel socket option ownership, but the description also names an IPv6 migration defect to be fixed separately while declared paths are IPv4-only. Clarify that cross-family CVE scope before reducing the record to its listed payload paths.
records.severity_review: HIGH to CRITICAL is substantive and preserved. The current CNA describes unauthenticated network attack paths and kernel memory corruption (CVSS 9.8). Both the IPv4 ownership defect and the separately mentioned IPv6 migration defect reside in running kernel socket lifetimes, not exported userspace header code. The exact header-only payload still passes, but no conclusion is made about the host kernel; deployment requires its separate assessment.

records.unchanged_applicability_basis: The description identifies server request waits that prevent closure and requires cancellation first. This is connection/request lifecycle behavior in the kernel SMB server; it does not describe a header or shared-library change.
Kernel packet clones share extension state whose reallocation invalidates stored pointers; the description preserves existing uAPI semantics rather than changing an exported header.

Expectation lists retain pointers into kernel connection extensions that can later move. The API atomicity discussion concerns kernel conntrack mutation, not exported-header or userspace implementation.

The parser incorrectly treats the complete response range and canonical layouts as each record's bounds. Fixes constrain kernel client parsing and preserve open behavior; references to context headers mean wire records, not exported C headers.
Changing kernel device flags invalidate a two-pass allocation count; a management caller receives the result but does not implement this unsafe fill.
The bounds failure is in the kernel L2CAP receive path over skb length. Received frame bytes trigger the parser but do not imply a userspace Bluetooth library defect.
A bare parent lookup lacks the operational hold that unlink later drops. Balancing that hold protects a live kernel socket connection; the defect is not a userspace Bluetooth API definition.
Different kernel connection-return paths fail to preserve the promised hold ownership; the fix balances internal references rather than userspace handles.
The VMM can trigger VM destruction, but the freed object and timer callback are kernel KVM state. The userspace VMM supplies the lifecycle event rather than the faulty implementation.

Despite the libiscsi name, the described consumer writes into kernel-managed scatterlists, pinned pages and page cache. The fix checks command direction in the kernel initiator; userspace write buffers are affected data, not the implementation.
Reentrant kernel group deletion invalidates a pointer-to-pointer iterator; RTM_GETMDB later exposes the state, but netlink is only a trigger.

Open vSwitch has userspace components, but this description identifies kernel conntrack expectation pointers invalidated by extension reallocation. It supplies no evidence that the userspace datapath shares this faulty implementation.

Adding extensions to the shared kernel conntrack entry invalidates expectation-list pointers. Resetting the shared entry during commit repairs packet-path ownership; shared here means packet clones, not shared userspace code.
Kernel skb destruction can precede payload release, so shared ring slots need separate completion ownership; shared data with userspace is not shared implementation code.
The record traces duplicate client cleanup to kfree in a kernel DRM open path. That concrete allocation/destruction path supports kernel implementation attribution despite the NVIF interface name.

Kernel DMA mapping failure leaves a scatterlist pointer after its owner unpins and frees the pages. Delaying assignment and clearing failure state repair MR ownership; socket operations only trigger that kernel path.
Kernel frame construction under-reserves space for VLAN plus lower-device headers; device-aware allocation is the affected operation.
The common helper operates on an skb and feeds kernel Open vSwitch checksum updates. Reuse by other kernel callers is not itself evidence of a shared userspace implementation.

Later chunks reuse a transport removed earlier in kernel packet processing, leaving association state with a dangling pointer. Discarding the remainder repairs protocol-object lifetime; no userspace parser or header implementation is identified.
The driver exposes a gap between kernel XArray lookup and xfrm_state reference acquisition; asynchronous firmware handling does not make this userspace code.
The out-of-range write targets a kernel queue map after device traffic-class reconfiguration. A sysfs write is the trigger, not a userspace implementation of the mapping allocator.

A concurrent link change alters required headroom between allocation and reservation. The kernel driver then writes outside its packet allocation; taking one snapshot is runtime synchronization, not an Ethernet-header definition change.
The affected internal helper sizes kernel skb headroom for tunnel callers; a header-only source location does not imply it is an exported linux-libc-dev header or userspace implementation.
Instruction selection occurs in the kernel BPF JIT at runtime. Compilation terminology and the mentioned test do not establish a kernel build-system or header-export effect.

Unsigned subtraction creates an invalid copy length in kernel skb helpers. Packet extension headers are parsed data; the affected implementation is kernel buffer management, not exported networking headers.
Kernel release paths use locking incompatible with accept handling and can free the same socket; accept is a syscall trigger, while the internal LLCP header supports lifecycle state.
The reference underflow arises when kernel timer cleanup races with handlers using transport/association objects. This lifetime ordering is not implemented by exported SCTP constants.

The allocation accepts a size the kernel destructor's signed index cannot represent. Restricting map creation prevents invalid kernel writes; BPF syscalls are inputs, not evidence that userspace headers execute the faulty loop.
The verifier treats packet memory as stable ordinary memory across a call that may invalidate it; this is kernel program validation, not exported pointer declarations.
The faulty runtime-generated access returns bits that contradict kernel verifier state. It is kernel BPF code generation, not a compiler or userspace-header build change.

The description explicitly identifies skb-backed BPF dynptr code as the only current consumer. Although the helper is in a header, its arithmetic governs kernel packet pointers and no userspace/shared consumer is identified.
Kernel verification aliases an invalid frame offset to a valid iterator slot through arithmetic; the BPF caller supplies input but not the validating implementation.

The freed object remains in the kernel DRM VMA interval tree and leaves synchronization resources alive. Device initialization failure triggers kernel object cleanup, not userspace graphics-library execution.

The offset underflow propagates into kernel skb checksum metadata and a network-driver copy. The described header helper has explicit kernel packet-processing consumers; the REMCSUM packet option is not itself an exported C header.
Concurrent kernel notification and configuration handlers can destroy an unrefcounted instance; socket close and UNBIND are triggers only.
The worker and garbage collector race over a kernel flow whose RCU reclamation becomes permitted too early. Status bits here synchronize runtime lifetime rather than define exported behavior.
Shared userspace libbpf and in-kernel CO-RE code. An affected libbpf1 package is present in the old image, so no current-image clearance is possible.
The queued kernel work keeps a pointer to an object freed by cancellation. Dequeueing before completion and avoiding lock recursion repair worker lifetime, not a userspace mesh library.
Kernel scan bookkeeping truncates or overflows device-reported zone counts; the zone data is an input rather than executable exported-header logic.
Both consumers access kernel allocator lists around RCU Tasks Trace callbacks. References to the generic list helper are call-trace context, not evidence of a userspace shared-library defect.

The operation is clearly kernel KVM state handling, but the sole supplied path is arch/s390/kvm/s390/interrupt.c. That repeated architecture component is a suspected path-attribution anomaly not substantiated by the short description; verify the exact source path before mapping payload absence.

The sizeof-on-void error underestimates the required response length and accepts an undersized output buffer in the kernel target. GCC behavior explains a runtime bounds-check defect, not a build/export vulnerability.
